{{short description|1847 hymn by Henry Francis Lyte}} {{About|the Christian hymn|other uses|Abide with Me (disambiguation)}} {{Use British English|date=July 2016}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2020}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = "Abide with Me" | type = [[Hymn]] | image = Abide_with_Me_Sheet_Music.png | alt = | caption = The hymn set to "Eventide" | occasion = | text = by [[Henry Francis Lyte]] | language = English | written = {{Start date|1847}} | based_on = {{Sourcetext|source=Bible|version=King James|book=Luke|chapter=24|verse=29}} | meter = 10 10 10 10 | melody = "Eventide" {{nowrap|by [[William Henry Monk]]}} | composed = {{Start date|1861}} | published = }}
"'''Abide with Me'''" is a Christian [[hymn]] by British [[Anglican]] [[cleric]] [[Henry Francis Lyte]] (1793–1847). A prayer for God to stay with the speaker throughout life and in death, it was written by Lyte in 1847 as he was dying from [[tuberculosis]]. It is most often sung to the tune "Eventide" by the English organist [[William Henry Monk]] (1823–1889).
==History== The author of the hymn, [[Henry Francis Lyte]], was an Anglican cleric. He was a curate in [[County Wexford]] from 1815 to 1818. According to a plaque erected in his memory in [[Taghmon]] Church, he preached frequently at the church in [[Killurin]], about nine miles from there. During that time the rector of Killurin Parish, the Reverend Abraham Swanne, was a lasting influence on Lyte's life and ministry. Later he was vicar of All Saints' Church in [[Brixham]], Devon, England. For most of his life Lyte suffered from poor health, and he would regularly travel abroad for relief, as was customary at that time.
There is some controversy as to the exact dating of the text to "Abide with Me". An article in ''The Spectator'', 3 October 1925, says that Lyte composed the hymn in 1820 while visiting a dying friend. It was related that Lyte was staying with the Hore family in County Wexford and had visited an old friend, William Augustus Le Hunte, who was dying. As Lyte sat with the dying man, William kept repeating the phrase "abide with me...". After leaving William's bedside, Lyte wrote the hymn and gave a copy of it to Le Hunte's family.
The belief is that when Lyte felt his own end approaching twenty-seven years later at the age of 54, as he developed [[tuberculosis]], he recalled the lines he had written so many years before in County Wexford. The Biblical link for the hymn is [[Gospel of Luke|Luke]] 24:29 in which the disciples asked Jesus to abide with them "for it is toward evening and the day is spent". Using his friend's more personal phrasing "Abide with Me", Lyte composed the hymn. His daughter, Anna Maria Maxwell Hogg, recounts the story of how "Abide with Me" came out of that context:
{{Blockquote| The summer was passing away, and the month of September (that month in which he was once more to quit his native land) arrived, and each day seemed to have a special value as being one day nearer his departure. His family were surprised and almost alarmed at his announcing his intention of preaching once more to his people. His weakness and the possible danger attending the effort, were urged to prevent it, but in vain. "It was better", as he used to say often playfully, when in comparative health, "to wear out than to rust out". He felt that he should be enabled to fulfil his wish, and feared not for the result. His expectation was well founded. He did preach, and amid the breathless attention of his hearers, gave them a sermon on the Holy Communion ... In the evening of the same day he placed in the hands of a near and dear relative the little hymn, "Abide with Me", with an air of his own composing, adapted to the words.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kidson |first1=Frank |title=Church and Organ Music: 'Abide With Me' |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xyk5AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA25 |work=The Musical Times |publisher=Novello |date=1 January 1908 |pages=24–25 |language=en}}</ref> }}
Just weeks later, on 20 November 1847 in [[Nice]], then in the [[Kingdom of Sardinia]], Lyte died. The hymn was sung for the first time at Lyte's funeral. Special thanksgiving services to mark Lyte's bicentenary were held in Taghmon and Killurin churches. Although Lyte wrote a tune for the hymn, the most usual tune for the hymn is "Eventide" by William Henry Monk.
==Lyrics== {{Wikisource}} The hymn is a prayer for God to remain present with the speaker throughout life, through trials, and through death. The opening line alludes to {{Bibleverse|Luke|24:29|KJV}}, "''Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent"'', and the penultimate verse draws on text from {{Bibleverse|1 Corinthians|15:55|KJV}}, ''"O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?"'':
{{Poem quote| Abide with me; fast falls the eventide; The darkness deepens; Lord with me abide. When other helpers fail and comforts flee, Help of the helpless, O abide with me.
Swift to its close ebbs out life's little day; Earth's joys grow dim; its glories pass away; Change and decay in all around I see; O Thou who changest not, abide with me.
Not a brief glance I beg, a passing word, But as Thou dwell'st with Thy disciples, Lord, Familiar, condescending, patient, free. Come not to sojourn, but abide with me.
Come not in terror, as the King of kings, But kind and good, with healing in Thy wings; Tears for all woes, a heart for every plea. Come, Friend of sinners, thus abide with me.
Thou on my head in early youth didst smile, And though rebellious and perverse meanwhile, Thou hast not left me, oft as I left Thee. On to the close, O Lord, abide with me.
I need Thy presence every passing hour. What but Thy grace can foil the tempter's power? Who, like Thyself, my guide and stay can be? Through cloud and sunshine, Lord, abide with me.
I fear no foe, with Thee at hand to bless; Ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness. Where is death's sting? Where, grave, thy victory? I triumph still, if Thou abide with me.
Hold Thou Thy cross before my closing eyes; Shine through the gloom and point me to the skies. Heaven's morning breaks, and earth's vain shadows flee; In life, in death, O Lord, abide with me.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.risa.co.uk/sla/song.php?songid=26985 |title=Abide with Me |publisher=Risa song lyrics archive |access-date=4 February 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180927194654/http://www.risa.co.uk/sla/song.php?songid=26985 |archive-date=2018-09-27}}</ref> }} Many hymnals omit some of the verses. For example, the compilers of one of the editions of ''[[Hymns Ancient and Modern]]'', of which William Henry Monk, the composer of the tune "Eventide", was the original editor, omitted the verse beginning ''"Thou on my head in early youth didst smile;"'' for being too personal.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bradley |first1=Ian |title=Abide with Me: The World of Victorian Hymns |year=1997 |url=https://archive.org/details/abidewithmeworld0000brad |url-access=registration |publisher=SCM Press Ltd |isbn=0-334-02703-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/abidewithmeworld0000brad/page/66 66]}}</ref>
==Tune== [[File:Abide With Me (1861).jpg|thumb|Abide with Me (1861)]] {{Listen | filename=Eventide.ogg | title="Eventide", by William Henry Monk | description=An organ performance of "Eventide," best known for its use with the hymn "Abide with Me," performed by Steven Dunlop. | format=[[Ogg]] }}
The [[hymn tune]] most often used with this hymn is "Eventide" composed by English organist and church musician [[William Henry Monk]] in 1861.<ref>{{cite web |title=Abide with Me |url=http://www.hymntime.com/tch/htm/a/b/i/d/abidewme.htm |publisher=The Cyber Hymnal |access-date=28 August 2010}}</ref>
Alternative tunes include: * "Abide with Me", Henry Lyte, 1847 * "Morecambe", Frederick C. Atkinson, 1870 * "Penitentia", [[Edward Dearle]], 1874 * unnamed, Samuel Liddle (1867-1951), published by Boosey & Co. in 1896; this is the version favoured by [[Dame Clara Butt]]. * "Woodlands", [[Walter Greatorex]], 1916
The principal theme of the fourth movement of [[Gustav Mahler]]'s [[Symphony No. 9 (Mahler)|Symphony No. 9]] is often noted for its similarity to Monk's "Eventide".<ref>{{citation |last=Mitchell |first=Donald |year=2002 |title=The Mahler Companion |publisher=OUP}}.</ref> [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]] composed a [[descant]] for the 1925 hymnal, [[Songs of Praise (hymnal)|''Songs of Praise'']];<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Kennedy |editor-first=Michael |date= 15 August 2013|title=The Oxford Dictionary of Music |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XX2sAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA2 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=2 |isbn=978-0199578542}}</ref> also an orchestral prelude ("Two Hymn-Tune Preludes", "1. Eventide") on the tune for the Hereford Festival of 1936.<ref>"The Works of Ralph Vaughan Williams", M. Kennedy, OUP</ref> The hymn was also set to music around 1890 by the American composer [[Charles Ives]], and was published in his collection ''Thirteen Songs'' in 1958, four years after his death.<ref>Ives, Charles E. ''Thirteen Songs'', New York: Peer International Corporation, 1958</ref>
==Popular usage== ===Religious services=== {{quote box | width=25% | align=right | quote="One of the most sung hymns at funerals, this is really a prayer to God to stay with him in death as He did with us in life." | source=—Hymns for Funerals by the BBC's ''[[Songs of Praise]]''.<ref name="funeral"/> }} The hymn is popular across many [[Christian denomination]]s and was said to have been a favourite of King [[George V]]<ref name=thefa.com>{{cite web |title=Abide with me |work=TheFA |url=http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/TheFACup/NewsAndFeatures/Postings/CupFinal_abide.htm |access-date=10 June 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080314125920/http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/TheFACup/NewsAndFeatures/Postings/CupFinal_abide.htm |archive-date=14 March 2008}}</ref><ref name="auto">Trevor Beeson (2009). [https://books.google.com/books?id=pUv8KoGELpQC&dq=%22abide+with+me%22&pg=PA37 "In Tuneful Accord: The Church Musicians"], SCM Press, p. 37.</ref> and [[Mahatma Gandhi]].<ref name="tt">{{cite news |url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/Beating-Retreat-weaves-soul-stirring-musical-evening/articleshow/7386283.cms |title=Beating Retreat weaves soul-stirring musical evening |date=29 January 2011 |work=The Times of India}}</ref> It became a legend{{clarify|date=July 2026}} that in 1947 it was sung at the [[Wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Philip Mountbatten|wedding of Queen Elizabeth II]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bryan |first1=Dora |title=Dora Bryan's Tapestry Tales |date=2005 |publisher=Hymns Ancient and Modern Ltd |page=45}}</ref> It is also often sung or played at Christian funerals;<ref name="funeral">{{cite news |title=Hymns for Funerals |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/39R8RR2r70McJnZwNBY6Lrm/hymns-for-funerals |access-date=8 November 2021 |agency=BBC}}</ref> notable examples include the funeral of [[Sun Yat-sen]] in 1925,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lundbom |first=Jack R. |url= |title=On the Road to Siangyang: Covenant Mission in Mainland China 1890–1949 |publisher=Pickwick Publications |year=2015 |isbn=978-1-4982-3529-7 |location=Eugene, Oregon |publication-date=2015 |pages=30 |language=en}}</ref> the [[Death and state funeral of George V|state funeral of George V]] in 1936,<ref>{{cite book |last=Range |first=Matthias |date=2016 |title=British Royal and State Funerals: Music and Ceremonial since Elizabeth I |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Kn1FDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA271 |location=Woodbridge, Suffolk |publisher=Boydell Press |page=268 |isbn=978-1783270927}}</ref> the [[Death and funeral of Mary of Teck|funeral of Queen Mary]] in 1953<ref>{{cite web|url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/50549294|title=Queen Mary buried at private Windsor service|work=[[The Courier-Mail]]|via=Trove|date=1 April 1953|accessdate=4 August 2023}}</ref> the state funeral of [[Jean, Grand Duke of Luxembourg]] in 2019, and the [[Death_and_state_funeral_of_Harald_V|state funeral of Harald V]] in 2026 <ref>{{cite AV media |date=2019 |title=Abide with me . Begräbnis von Großherzog Jean 4.5.2019 |type= |language=Luxembourgish |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FvaRSZWZ_v4 |access-date=4 August 2023 |location=www.youtube.com |publisher=sergeluxlu }}</ref> In 2019, ''[[Songs of Praise]]'' announced that ''Abide with Me'' was the fifth most popular hymn amongst British Christians.<ref>{{Cite web |title=‘Jerusalem’ voted the UK's favourite hymn |url=https://www.classicfm.com/music-news/jerusalem-named-britains-favourite-hymn/ |access-date=2025-08-22 |website=Classic FM |language=en}}</ref>
===Military services=== The hymn was sung at the service for the burial of the Unknown Warrior in Westminster Abbey in 1920.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Unknown Warrior |url=https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/unknown-warrior |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Westminster Abbey |language=en}}</ref> It is sometimes sung at the annual [[Anzac Day]] services in [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rsa.org.nz/remem/anzac_today.html |access-date=14 May 2006 |work=RSA |title=Remembrance – ANZAC Day |location=NZ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060424153725/http://www.rsa.org.nz/remem/anzac_today.html |archive-date=24 April 2006 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and in some [[Remembrance Day]] services in [[Canada]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vac-acc.gc.ca/content/feature/vetweek/comm_guide/CommGuide_e.pdf |access-date=8 October 2006 |title=A Guide to Commemorative Services |publisher=Veterans Affairs Canada |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060529040240/http://www.vac-acc.gc.ca/content/feature/vetweek/comm_guide/CommGuide_e.pdf |archive-date=29 May 2006}}</ref> and the [[United Kingdom]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Hymn: Abide with Me |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p05mfjx5 |access-date=8 November 2021 |agency=BBC}}</ref>
===Recordings=== The hymn has been widely recorded, by artists in various genres. [[Thelonious Monk]] arranged a version featuring [[John Coltrane]], [[Coleman Hawkins]], and [[Gigi Gryce]] in 1957.<ref>{{cite web|title="Thelonious Monk: Monk's Music" – "The first track is a horn-only, 55-second chart of the hymn 'Abide With Me'" |author=John Garratt|date=July 7, 2011|url=https://www.popmatters.com/140152-thelonious-monk-monks-music-2496042966.html|website=Popmatters.com}}</ref> Several versions have charted on the [[UK singles chart]]. In 1984, a version by [[the Inspirational Choir]], from their debut album ''[[Sweet Inspiration (The Inspirational Choir album)|Sweet Inspiration]]'', peaked at number 36,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/22195/inspirational-choir/ |title=INSPIRATIONAL CHOIR {{pipe}} full Official Chart History {{pipe}} Official Charts Company |website=Officialcharts.com}}</ref> and a re-release the following year also reached the same position.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/abide%20with%20me%20%7B1985%7D/|title=Abide with Me {1985} {{pipe}} full Official Chart History {{pipe}} Official Charts Company|website=Officialcharts.com}}</ref> A dance version by [[Vic Reeves]] reached number 47 in 1991,<ref name="auto1">{{cite web |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/abide-with-me/ |title=abide with me {{pipe}} full Official Chart History {{pipe}} Official Charts Company |website=Officialcharts.com}}</ref> which is from his sole album ''[[I Will Cure You]]''. In 2012, [[Emeli Sandé]] recorded her version for the [[2012 Summer Olympics]] on the soundtrack album ''[[Isles of Wonder (album)|Isles of Wonder]]''. It reached number 44 in the UK<ref name="auto1"/> and number 63 on the [[Irish Singles Chart]].<ref name="IRE">{{cite web |url=http://irish-charts.com/showinterpret.asp?interpret=Emeli+Sand%E9 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230521170448/http://irish-charts.com/showinterpret.asp?interpret=Emeli+Sand%EF%BF%BD |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 May 2023 |title=Discography Emeli Sandé |work=Irish Charts Portal |publisher=Hung Medien}}</ref> A 2013 version featuring [[Joe McElderry]] and the [[Royal Mail Choir]] was released as a charity single raising money for [[Prostate Cancer UK]], reaching number 19 on the [[UK Indie Chart]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/independent-singles-chart/20130421/130/ |title=Official Independent Singles Chart Top 50 |work=[[Official Charts Company]]}}</ref>
===In sport=== [[File:2011FACupFinalAbideWithMe.JPG|thumb|right|The Band of the [[Irish Guards]] playing "Abide with Me" prior to the [[2011 FA Cup Final]] at [[Wembley Stadium]], London]]
The first and last verses of the hymn are traditionally sung at the [[FA Cup]] Final about 15 minutes before the kick-off of the match.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.phrases.org.uk/meanings/22000.html |access-date=15 April 2009 |title=Abide with me |location=UK |publisher=Phrases |work=Meanings |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090403190135/http://www.phrases.org.uk/meanings/22000.html |archive-date=3 April 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The first formal use of the hymn was before the [[1927 FA Cup Final]] between [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] and [[Cardiff City]].
The association with the FA Cup Final goes back slightly further to the [[1923 FA Cup final|1923 final]] between [[Bolton Wanderers]] and [[West Ham United]] when record-breaking crowds spilled onto the pitch before kick-off. While the pitch was being cleared, the event choir, St Luke's, sang "Abide with Me"; the crowds of West Ham supporters walking back to the [[East End]] are also said to have sung the song. The choir's spontaneous recital may be the origin of the tradition of singing the song before cup finals.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/extra/bjy6eeo1gs/white-horse-final-100-years-on|title=White Horse Final: 100 years on |publisher=BBC |access-date=22 July 2023}}</ref>
The hymn has also been sung prior to the kick-off at every Rugby League [[Challenge Cup]] Final since 1929.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/100-years-of-rugby-league-from-the-great-divide-to-the-super-era-1597130.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220506/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/100-years-of-rugby-league-from-the-great-divide-to-the-super-era-1597130.html |archive-date=6 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=100 years of rugby league: From the great divide to the Super era |work=[[The Independent]] |access-date=12 August 2009 |last=Baker |first=Andrew |date=20 August 1995}}{{cbignore}}</ref>
It was featured in the [[2012 Summer Olympics opening ceremony|opening ceremony]] of the [[2012 London Olympics]], sung by [[Emeli Sandé]] as a tribute to the victims of the [[7 July 2005 London bombings|7/7 terrorist attacks]].<ref>{{cite web |title=William Henry Monk, Abide with me |url=https://www.classicfm.com/music-news/pictures/event/classical-music-opening-ceremony/emeli-sande-abide-me/ |website=Classic FM |access-date=1 February 2022}}</ref>
===In literature=== References in literature include [[George Orwell]]'s ''[[Burmese Days]]''.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Complete Works of George Orwell, Volume 2 |date=1986 |publisher=Secker & Warburg |page=117}}</ref>
The Victorian Poet Laureate [[Alfred, Lord Tennyson]], according to [[Francis Turner Palgrave]], on reading "Abide with Me", "was deeply impressed by its solemn beauty; remarking that it wanted very little to take rank among the really perfect poems of our language".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bradley |first1=Ian |title=Abide with Me: The World of Victorian Hymns |year=1997 |url=https://archive.org/details/abidewithmeworld0000brad |url-access=registration |publisher=SCM Press |isbn=0-334-02703-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/abidewithmeworld0000brad/page/207 207]}}</ref>
